title: An Insult Answered: War with Ammon and Aram
summary: When the Ammonite king Nahash dies, David sends envoys to console his son Hanun, but Hanun's officials convince him they are spies, and he humiliates them by shaving half their beards and cutting their garments at the hips. The Ammonites then hire Aramean armies, and Joab and Abishai defeat the coalition outside the Ammonite city. When Hadadezer brings reinforcements from beyond the Euphrates, David himself defeats them at Helam, and the Aramean kings make peace and become subject to Israel.
story: Chapter 9 showed David keeping faith with Saul's house; chapter 10 begins with David trying to keep faith with a foreign king and being rebuffed. The chapter gives a fuller account of the Aramean wars summarized in chapter 8, and it sets the stage for the most shameful chapter of David's life. The Ammonite war begun here is still going on in chapter 11, when David stays in Jerusalem while Joab besieges Rabbah, and it ends only in 12:26-31. The reader should keep this chapter in mind: the same king who sends his army into the field here will soon send one of his own soldiers to his death.
historical:
The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, around their capital Rabbah (Rabbath-ammon, the site of modern Amman in Jordan). Nahash was the Ammonite king who besieged Jabesh-gilead early in Saul's reign and was defeated by Saul (1 Samuel 11). The text doesn't say what kindness Nahash showed David. A common suggestion is that an enemy of Saul was a natural friend to Saul's rival, perhaps during David's years as a fugitive, but this is inference.

The Arameans were a network of kingdoms in Syria. Beth-rehob and Zobah lay to the north, Maacah near Mount Hermon, and Tob east of the Jordan. Hadadezer of Zobah appears as the head of a coalition that could draw troops from beyond the Euphrates (verse 16). Helam, the site of the second battle, was east of the Jordan, though its exact location is uncertain. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 19 adds that the Ammonites paid a thousand talents of silver for the hired chariots, and some of its numbers differ from those in Samuel, a common feature of numbers in copied ancient texts.
cultural:
Sending comforters on a king's death was a normal courtesy between allied rulers, and part of the ongoing diplomacy that kept treaties alive under a new king. The Ammonite princes' suspicion was not absurd either, since envoys did gather intelligence. What makes Hanun's response so provocative is its form. A full beard was a mark of a grown man's dignity in Israel and among its neighbors, and shaving half of it made each envoy ridiculous. Cutting their garments at the hips exposed them in the way captives were stripped and paraded (compare Isaiah 20:4). To insult a king's envoys was to insult the king who sent them, and everyone involved understood it as an act of war.

David's order that the men wait in Jericho until their beards grew back spared them the shame of returning to the capital in that state. Jericho was the first town west of the Jordan on the road from Ammon. The phrase "a stench to David" (verse 6) is an idiom for becoming hateful to someone.
literary: The chapter has two movements, each built around a battle, and a closing summary. Its center is Joab's speech in verses 11-12, the most memorable lines in the chapter. Joab, facing enemies before and behind, splits the army with his brother, promises mutual rescue, and commits the outcome to God: "May the LORD do what is good in His sight." The chapter is carefully symmetrical: the Ammonites see and flee, the Arameans see and regroup, the vassal kings see and make peace. The repeated verb see (verses 6, 9, 14, 15, 19) marks each turn of the story, as each party reads the situation and acts on what it sees.

outline.t: Joab and Abishai fight on two fronts
David defeats Hadadezer's reinforcements at Helam

doctrines.note: Joab plans carefully and fights hard, then leaves the result with God: "May the LORD do what is good in His sight." The chapter holds human responsibility and divine sovereignty together without resolving the tension.

Hanun's disaster begins with suspicion. His advisers read a gesture of kindness as a plot, and the insult that follows draws his people into a war they lose. Pride and distrust are shown doing their damage on a national scale.

words.note: Chazaq, to be strong or strengthen. Joab's charge "Be strong" (verse 12) echoes the words spoken to Joshua before the conquest (Joshua 1:6-9). It is a call to courage rooted in loyalty to God's people, not a boast in human power.

Yeshuah, salvation or rescue. The BSB renders it rescue in verse 11, where Joab and Abishai promise to come to each other's help. In the Psalms the same word often describes God's deliverance; here it is used of soldiers who owe each other their lives.

Chesed, kindness or loyal love. David wants to repay Nahash's chesed to Hanun (verse 2), the same word that governed his treatment of Mephibosheth in chapter 9. This time loyal love is refused, and the refusal has consequences.

Baash, to stink. The Ammonites "had become a stench to David" (verse 6), an idiom for becoming odious or hateful. The same vivid idiom appears elsewhere in Samuel when Saul's attack makes Israel a stench to the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:4).

christ: This chapter is a war story, and its link to Christ is thematic rather than predictive. It shows kindness offered and scorned, and the painful results of reading good will as hostility. The Gospels tell of a king who sent messengers, and finally his son, to those who treated them shamefully (Mark 12:1-9). Joab's words, "May the LORD do what is good in His sight," also anticipate the posture Jesus took before the cross, praying that the Father's will be done. The chapter doesn't picture those events, but it helps a reader feel the weight of a rejected envoy.
questions: Hanun's advisers read kindness as a trick. When have you misjudged someone's good intentions, and what did it cost?
David protected his humiliated men from further shame by letting them wait in Jericho. How can you protect the dignity of someone who has been humiliated?
Joab planned carefully and then said, “May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” How do you hold careful planning and trust in God together?
